analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime to switch someone's phone company without their consent.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: In the late 1990s, phone companies sometimes switched a customer's local or long-distance carrier without permission — a practice known as slamming. This bill would have made that a federal crime, with fines and short jail terms for individuals and fines up to $200,000 for phone carriers who do it repeatedly. It also ordered the Attorney General to study how these frauds happen and what they cost consumers. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Telephone subscribers whose local or long-distance service could be switched without their knowledge or consent. The bill gave them a federal criminal remedy against the people and companies that switch phone service in violation of Federal Communications Commission consent procedures, and promised a government study documenting the cost of that fraud to consumers and the marketplace [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It makes it a federal crime for any person to submit a request to change someone's telephone exchange or toll service in willful violation of the FCC's procedures, punishable by up to a $1,000 fine and 30 days in jail for a first offense and up to a $10,000 fine and 9 months for repeat offenses [S3].
It imposes fines of up to $50,000 on telecommunications carriers for a first conviction and up to $200,000 for a subsequent conviction when they submit or execute an unauthorized carrier change [S3].

It directs the Attorney General to study and report to Congress on fraudulent and criminal behavior by carriers and their agents in soliciting, marketing, and assigning wire services, including the costs this fraud imposes on consumers and the marketplace [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Telecommunications carriers and their sales agents, who would face federal criminal fines — and in the case of individuals, jail time — for switching a customer's phone service without following the FCC's consent procedures. Carriers that profited from moving customers to new service without permission would lose that revenue.

drawbacks.text: The penalties for individuals are modest — a $1,000 fine and up to 30 days in jail for a first offense — which a skeptic could call too light to deter a practice worth far more to carriers than the penalty [S3].

The FCC already had civil and regulatory enforcement tools against slamming; adding criminal liability for violations of agency procedures raises the question of whether ordinary telemarketing mistakes could be swept into federal criminal court, a concern an honest supporter would have to address [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, documented consumer harm — unauthorized switches of phone service that cost people money and market trust — with targeted criminal penalties aimed at the companies and agents that profit from it. Its main weaknesses are the light first-offense penalties and the possibility of criminalizing conduct that regulators could handle civilly. On balance it was a narrow, low-cost consumer protection measure, but it was never debated, so its design was never tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on October 29, 1997, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee that same day [S1] [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died at the end of the 105th Congress [S5] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Telecommunications carriers and telemarketing agents who switched customers' phone service without consent were better off: they faced no new federal criminal penalties, and the practice continued under civil regulation alone. Consumers who were slammed gained nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and committee agendas in the 105th Congress
against.what_they_did: Controlled which bills received committee time and floor action; none was given to this bill and no Republican cosponsored it

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split shows up in the record; its only support was a single Democrat and it drew zero cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: Carriers and their agents made money by moving customers to new phone service without clear consent; the bill would have imposed federal criminal fines of up to $200,000 on carriers for doing so. Blocking the bill preserved that revenue stream and left consumers to rely on civil regulatory enforcement [S3] [S2].

Sales agents who submitted unauthorized carrier-change requests would have faced federal fines and up to 30 days in jail for a first offense. The bill's death left them subject only to FCC civil procedures [S3].
